paragraphs.heading: Rivers in the sea
paragraphs.text: An ocean current is a steady, directed flow of seawater. Forces such as wind, breaking waves, and differences in temperature and salinity drive it. The shape of the sea floor and coastline, along with other currents, steer its direction and strength. Currents are measured in sverdrups (Sv), where 1 Sv is a flow of 1,000,000 m³ of water every second.

paragraphs.heading: Surface and deep
paragraphs.text: There are two main kinds: surface currents and deep-water currents. Surface currents are mostly driven by wind; big prevailing winds drive major lasting currents, while seasonal or occasional winds drive currents that last about as long as those winds do. Deep-water currents are driven by differences in density, which come from changes in temperature and salinity. Currents flow sideways across whole oceans and also up and down, and this upwelling and downwelling carries nutrients and gases, carbon dioxide among them, between the surface and the deep.

paragraphs.heading: The global conveyor belt
paragraphs.text: The density-driven part is called the thermohaline circulation: "thermo" refers to temperature and "haline" to salt, which together set seawater's density. It is also known as the global conveyor belt. Surface currents such as the Gulf Stream travel from the equatorial Atlantic toward the poles, cool on the way, and sink at high latitudes to form North Atlantic Deep Water. This dense water spreads into the ocean basins; most of it rises again in the Southern Ocean, but the oldest water, around 1000 years in transit, comes up in the North Pacific.

paragraphs.heading: Moving heat around the world
paragraphs.text: On their way, these water masses carry heat and matter, including dissolved substances and gases, around the planet, so the state of the circulation strongly affects Earth's climate. Currents change the temperature of the regions they pass. Warm currents along temperate coasts heat the sea breezes blowing over them. The Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Drift, make northwest Europe much milder than other places at the same high latitude, while the Humboldt Current gives Lima, Peru, a cooler climate than the tropics around it.

paragraphs.heading: Drifts, currents and streams
paragraphs.text: Currents are sorted by temperature into warm and cold ones, and by speed, size and direction into drifts, currents and streams. Drifts, like the North Atlantic Drift, are surface water pushed forward by the prevailing wind. Currents, like the Labrador Current, move faster than drifts and in a clearer direction. Streams, like the Gulf Stream, move larger masses of water faster still.

paragraphs.heading: The biggest current
paragraphs.text: The largest current of all is the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, a wind-driven flow that circles Antarctica clockwise without a break. It links all the ocean basins, and water rising and sinking on either side of it connects the atmosphere to the deep ocean. Since the 2000s, an international program called Argo has used a fleet of automated floats drifting with the currents to map the ocean's temperature and salinity. What it gathers will help explain the ocean's role in Earth's climate.
